messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaito had always been drawn to the thrill of capturing life's most intense moments through his lens. As a photographer, he had spent years honing his craft, but nothing could have prepared him for the combat zone where he was deployed at 17. It was there that he witnessed the devastating loss of his unit, and the memory of that day has haunted him ever since. For Kaito, the event feels more real than any ordinary memory – the smells, the sounds, the screams. When triggered without warning by something as innocuous as a helicopter overhead or the smell of smoke from a BBQ, he is instantly transported back to that fateful day. The rage that follows is overwhelming, leaving him breathless and trembling with anger. As Kaito struggles to make sense of what happened, he has come to believe that people can't be trusted – not even himself. He feels like he failed to protect his comrades, a weight that presses down on him daily. "I should have done more," he tells himself, over and over. This self-doubt seeps into every aspect of his life, leaving him feeling like he no longer belongs anywhere. This sense of disconnection and mistrust fuels Kaito's growing threat monitoring system. He finds himself constantly on edge, unable to relax even in the safety of his own home. Every creak of the floorboards or unexpected noise sends him into high alert, his senses heightened as if anticipating another attack. In a misguided attempt to regain control, he has started taking risks that could put him and others in harm's way – driving recklessly, exploring abandoned buildings at night. As Kaito's world shrinks under the weight of these threats, his memories of the event grow stronger. He becomes convinced that he is walking on borrowed time, that danger lurks around every corner. This perpetual state of hypervigilance has started to affect his work as a photographer – he can no longer focus on capturing the beauty in the world when all he sees is potential threats. Kaito's loved ones have noticed the change in him too. His friends and family try to reach out, but Kaito pushes them away, convinced that they couldn't possibly understand what he's going through. He feels like a ghost drifting through life, invisible and untouchable. One day, while on assignment at a crowded market, Kaito's startle response was triggered by the sound of a vendor slamming down a tray. The resulting panic attack left him shaken, his equipment scattered across the pavement. It was then that he realized he needed help – not just to cope with his memories but to rebuild a sense of purpose and belonging in a world that now seemed too bright, too loud, and too full of unknown dangers. As Kaito sat in his darkened apartment, surrounded by the eerie glow of his camera equipment, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was living on borrowed time. He knew it was time to seek help, not just for himself but for those who still cared about him – before his world shrunk any further and he lost himself completely in the abyss of his own fears.
